title: The gift of the astras
hookLine: the morning after the forest is freed, the sage hands over everything he has
carry: the guru gives mantras to the ready

cards: They spend the night in the freed forest. In the morning, Vishvamitra is smiling. He has watched this boy ask before acting, obey without sulking, try mercy before force.
Now the sage decides to hand over everything he has. Not land, not gold. Something no treasury holds, and no army could take from him.
Sit down, he tells Rama, and get ready.

teach.h: AN ASTRA: A GOD'S POWER ON A WORD.
teach.b: What Vishvamitra gives are the astras, the divine weapons. An astra isn't just an arrow. It's a power called up by a mantra and released through a weapon: the force of a god, carried on a word.
The sage names them one after another, and the list runs on for verses. The discus of dharma and the discus of time. Indra's thunderbolt.
The weapon of Brahma himself. The noose of Varuna, lord of the waters. The fire weapon, the wind weapon, and one called manava, named for Manu, the first human.
As he recites, the weapons appear, not as metal but as shining beings, standing before Rama with palms joined. We are yours, they say. Tell us what to do.
Rama touches each one and answers simply: stay in my mind, and come when I need you. And look when they're given.
Not on day one, but after a test, once the sage has seen how this young man uses force. Hindu tradition still keeps this pattern.
A mantra is traditionally received from a teacher, often at an initiation, when the teacher judges the student ready; that readiness is called adhikara.

In many families, a boy's sacred-thread ceremony is when he's first given the Gayatri mantra, and the Gayatri is traditionally credited to Vishvamitra himself. The power waits for the person. It doesn't come first.

how: In the epics, astras are given by teachers or gods to those judged worthy, invoked by mantra; in the same way, Hindu families and teachers traditionally hand on a mantra, such as the Gayatri at the sacred-thread ceremony, when the student is ready.

games.q: you're Vishvamitra. you hold powers carried on mantras, and a young prince has just passed his first test. when do you hand them over?
o: never; they're too dangerous for anyone.
now, because he's shown he's ready.
on the first day, to anyone who asks.
games.why: he gives them after Tataka, once he's seen how Rama uses force. mantras pass from guru to a student judged ready.

practice: Many Hindus keep one mantra close: a name of God or a line received from a teacher or a parent, repeated quietly, a practice called japa. Sit, and repeat silently one sacred word you were given: Om, a name, a line your family says.
If you don't have one, let the breath itself be the word. Don't send it anywhere. Ask it, the way Rama asked his, to stay in your mind and come when it's truly needed.

wordCard.voice: The weapons. The astras, divine powers carried on mantras, which Vishvamitra gives Rama after Tataka, and which wait on his mind.

orig.note: Sanskrit astra: a weapon that is released or hurled, in the epics a divine power called up by mantra.

carryVoice: Your line: the guru gives mantras to the ready. The power waits until the person is. Day five hundred two, done.
